messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Malia first traveled to the conflict zone at twenty-seven, a year out of graduate school, eager to put her training in crisis intervention to use. She was assigned to a field hospital on the outskirts of a city that had been under siege for months. What she remembers now is fragmented—the way dust coated everything, the constant hum of generators, the smell of burnt metal and something sweet she could never identify. But the parts she cannot reach are the ones that haunt her most. There are entire stretches of those weeks that feel like a locked room in her mind. When she tries to deliberately recall what happened during the worst of the shelling, her thoughts skid away, and she finds herself pushing the memory back before it can fully form. It is as if her own brain has walled off the worst of it, and she both resents and relies on that protection.

Now, at thirty, Malia works as a parole officer in a midsized American city. The job was supposed to be a return to order—structured meetings, paperwork, predictable routines. Instead, it has become a daily minefield. The taste of the instant coffee in the breakroom sometimes triggers a visceral lurch in her stomach; it reminds her of the sweet, cloying drinks she was given by local aid workers who tried to keep her hydrated. She has learned to bring her own tea. More difficult to manage are the moments when a client raises their voice in her office. Even calm expressions of frustration—a clenched jaw, a raised hand in explanation—send a surge of heat through her chest. She has come to believe that anger is always one step away from violence, that any man who raises his voice is about to become the men she saw screaming orders in the triage tent.

The victim memories are the hardest. When she reviews a client’s file and reads about a robbery or an assault, she sees not a crime report but the faces of the wounded she could not save. One man in his forties, recently released and mandated to meet with her weekly, reminds her of a medic she worked alongside who was killed by shrapnel. She cannot look at him without her throat tightening. She has started scheduling his appointments for late in the day so she can go home immediately afterward.

Over the months, Malia has built a quiet architecture of avoidance. She never eats lunch in the communal kitchen, where the smell of reheated food might trigger the taste memory. She keeps her office door closed and conducts meetings with her back to the window, because the sound of a car backfiring outside makes her flinch. She has stopped attending team meetings where colleagues discuss their caseloads with passion; she tells herself she is too busy, but the truth is that their raised voices, even in animated agreement, feel like a threat.

The consequences have accumulated. Her supervisor has noted her withdrawal and asked if she is overwhelmed. Malia said no. She has stopped seeing friends, because she cannot explain why the smell of grilled meat at a barbecue makes her excuse herself to the bathroom. Her divorce, finalized a year ago, was partly a casualty of this silence—her ex-husband could not understand why she would freeze when he argued about grocery bills.

What finally brought Malia to seek help was a moment last week. She was driving home and passed a food truck selling street meat. The gustatory memory hit her so hard she had to pull over, her mouth filling with the phantom taste of that sweet drink, her hands shaking on the wheel. She sat in the car for twenty minutes, unable to remember how to get home. That night, she searched online for a therapist who specializes in trauma. She is terrified that the locked room in her mind is going to break open, and even more terrified that it will stay sealed forever, leaving her stranded in a life she no longer recognizes.
